title: The sandals come down
hookLine: the coronation; the sandals come down; what a serial leaves behind
carry: hanuman listens wherever rama's story is told

lines: FROM A KING WITH NO SONS...
cards: The last episode of a series that ran for weeks. The credits. Then a strange quiet in the room, like someone moved out.
Five weeks ago, this started with an old king who had no sons. Then four boys, a bow nobody could lift, Sita choosing. Kaikeyi's two wishes.
Fourteen years. A brother who put sandals on a throne. A golden deer, a line in the dust, an old bird who tried.
Shabari's berries. A bridge, a squirrel, a foot nobody could move, a giant who woke, ten heads, a fire. Lamps.

teach.b: Remember the sandals? Fourteen years ago, Bharata refused the throne, set Rama's sandals on it, and ruled as their servant. Now, in the story, he brings them back and places them on Rama's feet himself.
I've kept your kingdom, he says, in effect; here it is. A brother handing back what was never his. Then the coronation.

teach.h: THE CORONATION, HANUMAN AT HIS FEET.
teach.b: Rama sits on the throne with Sita beside him, the brothers around them, and Hanuman at his feet.
The story says Rama's reign was a time when there was no fear, no untimely death, when the rains came on time.
People still say Ram Rajya, the rule of Rama, to mean a just and peaceful society, and people still argue about what that should look like. Valmiki's story doesn't stop cleanly here.

There's another book after this one, with some of the hardest chapters in the whole Ramayana, and you'll meet them later on the path. But this serial ends at the coronation. So what does a serial leave behind?

teach.h: WHEREVER THE STORY IS TOLD, HANUMAN LISTENS.
teach.b: In the Uttara Kanda, as the allies take their leave, Hanuman asks Rama for one thing: to stay alive on earth for as long as the story of Rama is told. Tradition says he's still here, one of the deathless ones, listening.

That's why families read the Ramayana aloud at home and in temples, and at some readings a seat is left empty for him: wherever Rama's name is sung, Hanuman is said to come. The ending isn't really the end.

how: Images of Rama's coronation (Rama pattabhishekam), with Sita beside him and Hanuman at his feet, hang in Hindu homes; at some Ramayana readings and recitations a seat is left for Hanuman, who tradition says is present wherever the story is told.

o: a sequel where Rama goes back into the forest
what stays after the end: a crown, and a story told
the war that follows Rama's return to the city

s: Valmiki's Ramayana ends with the coronation
there's another book after it, the Uttara Kanda, with some of the hardest chapters.
Hanuman asked to live as long as Rama's story is told
and tradition says he's still here, listening.
Bharata kept the throne for himself
he ruled as the sandals' servant and gave the kingdom back.

games.q: you're Hanuman. the war is over, the allies are going home, and you can ask Rama for one thing. what do you ask for?
o: to live as long as Rama's story is told.
to go home to Kishkindha in peace.
games.why: he asks to stay on earth for as long as the story of Rama is told. tradition says he's still here, wherever it's read.

practice: Rama's name itself is a prayer. Many Hindus repeat it softly, Sita Ram, Sita Ram, or simply Ram, a practice called japa: repeating a holy name.
For two minutes, if you pray, say it quietly with your breath, and picture Hanuman sitting nearby, listening.
If you don't pray, let one character from these five weeks sit with you instead, Jatayu, Shabari, the squirrel, Bharata with the sandals, and notice what stayed.

wordCard.voice: After. The sandals come down, the king is crowned, and Hanuman stays as long as the story is told.

orig.note: Sanskrit: paduka, a sandal. Rama's padukas ruled Ayodhya for fourteen years.

carryVoice: Your line: Hanuman listens wherever Rama's story is told. Seventy days, one whole epic. Tomorrow, a new story, and a much bigger family.
